claim: C. elegans heterochromatin proteins HPL-2/HP1, LIN-13, LIN-61, LET-418/Mi-2, and MET-2/SETDB1 act together with the piRNA and nuclear RNAi pathways to silence repetitive elements and prevent genotoxic stress in the germ line.
source: Here we show that a diverse set of C. elegans heterochromatin proteins act together with the piRNA and nuclear RNAi pathways to silence repetitive elements and prevent genotoxic stress in the germ line.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript including ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, genetic interactions, and functional assays.

claim: Mutants in genes encoding HPL-2/HP1, LIN-13, LIN-61, LET-418/Mi-2, and H3K9me2 histone methyltransferase MET-2/SETDB1 show functionally redundant sterility.
source: Mutants in genes encoding HPL-2/HP1, LIN-13, LIN-61, LET-418/Mi-2, and H3K9me2 histone methyltransferase MET-2/SETDB1 also show functionally redundant sterility, increased germline apoptosis, DNA repair defects, and interactions with small RNA pathways.
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 1 demonstrating synthetic sterility in double mutant combinations.

claim: Fertility of heterochromatin mutants could be partially restored by inhibiting cep-1/p53.
source: Remarkably, fertility of heterochromatin mutants could be partially restored by inhibiting cep-1/p53, endogenous meiotic double strand breaks, or the expression of MIRAGE1 DNA transposons.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi and genetic experiments shown in Figure 4 where cep-1 inhibition increases brood size of heterochromatin mutants.

claim: Fertility of heterochromatin mutants could be partially restored by inhibiting endogenous meiotic double strand breaks.
source: Remarkably, fertility of heterochromatin mutants could be partially restored by inhibiting cep-1/p53, endogenous meiotic double strand breaks, or the expression of MIRAGE1 DNA transposons.
evidence: Demonstrated by spo-11 RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A where inhibiting meiotic DSBs increases fertility.

claim: Fertility of heterochromatin mutants could be partially restored by inhibiting the expression of MIRAGE1 DNA transposons.
source: Remarkably, fertility of heterochromatin mutants could be partially restored by inhibiting cep-1/p53, endogenous meiotic double strand breaks, or the expression of MIRAGE1 DNA transposons.
evidence: Demonstrated by MIRAGE1 RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A where knockdown of MIRAGE1 increases fertility of hpl-2, let-418, and lin-13 mutants.

claim: Heterochromatin is less transcriptionally active than euchromatin and highly enriched for repetitive elements such as transposons and satellite repeats.
source: It is less transcriptionally active than euchromatin and highly enriched for repetitive elements such as transposons and satellite repeats, which are kept silent to maintain genome integrity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about heterochromatin properties.

claim: In C. elegans, heterochromatin associated histone methylations H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 are mostly found in many small domains on the distal arm regions of autosomal chromosomes.
source: In C. elegans, heterochromatin associated histone methylations H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 are instead mostly found in many small domains on the distal arm regions of autosomal chromosomes (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011 and confirmed by the ChIP-seq data in this study shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The SETDB1 homolog MET-2 carries out mono- and di-methylation of H3K9.
source: The SETDB1 homolog MET-2 carries out mono- and di-methylation of H3K9.
evidence: Supported by citation to Towbin et al., 2012 in the following sentence.

claim: SET-25 primarily carries out tri-methylation of H3K9, but it can generate all three methylated forms of H3K9.
source: SET-25 primarily carries out tri-methylation of H3K9, but it can generate all three methylated forms of H3K9.
evidence: Supported by citation to Towbin et al., 2012 in the following sentence.

claim: In the absence of both MET-2 and SET-25, H3K9 methylation is undetectable.
source: In the absence of both proteins, H3K9 methylation is undetectable, heterochromatic distal arm regions show reduced association with the nuclear lamina, and heterochromatic transgenes are desilenced (Towbin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Towbin et al., 2012.

claim: HP1 contains a chromodomain that binds to methylated H3K9.
source: HP1 contains a chromodomain that binds to methylated H3K9, and it is essential for heterochromatin maintenance (Zeng et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2010.

claim: HPL-2 and LIN-61 can bind to all methylated forms of H3K9 in vitro.
source: Both HPL-2 and LIN-61 can bind to all methylated forms of H3K9 in vitro (Koester-Eiserfunke and Fischle, 2011; Garrigues et al., 2015; Studencka et al., 2012), and both can repress a heterochromatic reporter (Towbin et al., 2012; Couteau et al., 2002; Harrison et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A complex containing LIN-13, HPL-2, and LIN-61 has been detected in vivo.
source: A complex containing LIN-13, HPL-2, and LIN-61 has been detected in vivo, and LIN-13 is required for the formation of HPL-2::GFP nuclear foci (Wu et al., 2012; Coustham et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2012 and Coustham et al., 2006.

claim: LET-418 is an ortholog of Mi-2, an ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling component of the repressive NuRD and Mec complexes.
source: LET-418 is an ortholog of Mi-2, an ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling component of the repressive NuRD and Mec complexes (von Zelewsky et al., 2000; Unhavaithaya et al., 2002; Passannante et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: let-418 and lin-13 null mutants are sterile.
source: let-418 and lin-13 null mutants are sterile (von Zelewsky et al., 2000; Meléndez and Greenwald, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to von Zelewsky et al., 2000 and Meléndez and Greenwald, 2000.

claim: hpl-2 null mutants show temperature sensitive sterility.
source: hpl-2 null mutants show temperature sensitive sterility (Schott et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schott et al., 2006.

claim: lin-61 and met-2 null mutants have slightly reduced brood sizes.
source: lin-61 and met-2 null mutants have slightly reduced brood sizes (Koester-Eiserfunke and Fischle, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koester-Eiserfunke and Fischle, 2011.

claim: hpl-2 mutants produce abnormal oocytes, suggesting defective gametogenesis.
source: The underlying cause of the fertility defects is not known, but hpl-2 mutants have been shown to produce abnormal oocytes, suggesting defective gametogenesis (Couteau et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Couteau et al., 2002 and confirmed by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: An HPL-2 ChIP-chip study in early embryos showed that most binding was on the distal arm regions of autosomes in a pattern similar to H3K9me1 and H3K9me2.
source: An HPL-2 ChIP-chip study in early embryos showed that most binding was on the distal arm regions of autosomes in a pattern of similar to H3K9me1 and H3K9me2; interestingly, binding to chromatin was not dependent on H3K9 methylation (Garrigues et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garrigues et al., 2015.

claim: SETDB1 binds to promoters of developmentally regulated genes in mammalian embryonic stem cells, 40% of which are found next to or overlapping endogenous retroviruses.
source: SETDB1 binds to promoters of developmentally regulated genes in mammalian embryonic stem cells, 40% of which are found next to or overlapping endogenous retroviruses (Yuan et al., 2009; Karimi et al., 2011; Bilodeau et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yuan et al., 2009; Karimi et al., 2011; Bilodeau et al., 2009.

claim: Retrotransposons are derepressed in Setdb1 knockout mouse ES cell lines and primordial germ cells.
source: In addition, retrotransposons are derepressed in Setdb1 knockout mouse ES cell lines and primordial germ cells (Karimi et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karimi et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Retrotransposons are repressed by HP1α and HP1β in mESCs, but it is a different set of retrotransposons than is targeted by SETDB1.
source: Retrotransposons are also repressed by HP1α and HP1β in mESCs, but it is a different set of retrotransposons than is targeted by SETDB1 (Maksakova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maksakova et al., 2013.

claim: The piRNA pathway involves generation of 21nt piRNAs that bind to the Piwi argonaute protein PRG-1 in C. elegans.
source: In the C. elegans germ line, the piRNA pathway involves generation of 21nt piRNAs that bind to the Piwi argonaute protein PRG-1 (Wang and Reinke, 2008; Das et al., 2008; Batista et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang and Reinke, 2008; Das et al., 2008; Batista et al., 2008.

claim: The piRNA pathway triggers generation of secondary 22G siRNAs that mediate silencing either in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
source: This triggers generation of secondary 22G siRNAs that mediate silencing either in the cytoplasm or nucleus (Ashe et al., 2012; Das et al., 2008; Shirayama et al., 2012; Luteijn et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Guang et al., 2010; Gu et al., 2009, 2012; Burton et al., 2011; Burkhart et al., 2011; Buckley et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The nuclear RNAi pathway orchestrates H3K9 and H3K27 methylation and/or inhibition of RNA Pol II.
source: In the nucleus, the piRNA pathway engages a second small RNA pathway called the nuclear RNAi pathway (or nrde pathway), which orchestrates H3K9 and H3K27 methylation and/or inhibition of RNA Pol II (Guang et al., 2010; Burkhart et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2015; Alló and Kornblihtt, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guang et al., 2010; Burkhart et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2015; Alló and Kornblihtt, 2010.

claim: Regions transcriptionally upregulated in hrde-1 mutants were found to be enriched for retrotransposons.
source: Regions transcriptionally upregulated in hrde-1 mutants were found to be enriched for retrotransposons, suggesting that repetitive elements may be endogenous targets in the germ line (Ni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ni et al., 2014.

claim: All pairs of hpl-2, lin-13, lin-61, let-418, and met-2 show genetic interactions in fertility.
source: All pairs of hpl-2, lin-13, lin-61, let-418, and met-2 show genetic interactions in fertility, as determined in this study or previous studies.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi and double mutant experiments shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: HPL-2, LET-418, LIN-13, LIN-61, and MET-2 are enriched on the distal arm regions of autosomes.
source: Binding of each of the five factors is enriched on the distal arm regions of the autosomes (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HPL-2, LET-418, LIN-13, LIN-61, and MET-2 show similar binding patterns genome-wide.
source: Examination of ChIP-seq signals at a more local level revealed similar binding patterns for the five heterochromatin proteins (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq tracks shown in Figure 2B and correlation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Signals for each of the five heterochromatin factors showed high correlation with H3K9me2 but not with H3K9me3.
source: In addition, signals for each of the five heterochromatin factors showed high correlation with H3K9me2 but not with H3K9me3 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 58% of sites in the Any5 peak set are bound by more than one heterochromatin factor.
source: There is a high degree of peak overlap among the five factors, with 58% of sites in the Any5 set being bound by >1 factor (Figure 2C).
evidence: Calculated from peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The largest binding group contains all five heterochromatin factors (termed 'All5').
source: Strikingly, the largest binding group contains all five factors (termed 'All5'; Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown in the UpSet plot in Figure 2C where the All5 class has 4810 peaks.

claim: A large proportion of each heterochromatin factor's peaks overlaps a repeat sequence (46.3–71.0%).
source: A large proportion of each factor's peaks overlaps a repeat sequence (46.3–71.0%), and regions with all five factors have particularly strong repeat association (76.6%, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Calculated from peak and repeat overlap analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Of the total set of 62331 annotated repetitive elements, nearly half (46%) overlap a peak of at least one heterochromatin factor.
source: Furthermore, of the total set of 62331 annotated repetitive elements, nearly half (46%) overlap a peak of at least one factor, and 8002 (13%) overlap all five factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Calculated from repeat and peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HPL-2, LIN-13, LIN-61, MET-2, and H3K9me2 have a particularly strong association with Helitron families.
source: HPL-2, LIN-13, LIN-61, MET-2, and H3K9me2 have a particularly strong association with Helitron families; LET-418 shows generally lower enrichment on repeat families than the other factors (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplements 2–6).
evidence: Demonstrated by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: H3K9me2 is more associated with DNA transposons and satellite repeats, whereas H3K9me3 is particularly associated with retrotransposon families, especially LINE and SINE elements.
source: H3K9me2 is more associated with DNA transposons and satellite repeats, similar to the heterochromatin factors, whereas H3K9me3 is particularly associated with retrotransposon families, especially LINE and SINE elements (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplements 7–8).
evidence: Demonstrated by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplements 7–8.

claim: H3K9me2 and all heterochromatin factors are enriched at telomeres, whereas H3K9me3 is not.
source: We also observed that H3K9me2 and all heterochromatin factors are enriched at telomeres, whereas H3K9me3 is not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by telomere enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Repetitive elements are upregulated in hpl-2, let-418, lin-13, lin-61, and met-2 set-25 mutants.
source: We observed upregulation of repetitive elements in every mutant strain (hpl-2, let-418, lin-13, lin-61, and met-2 set-25) (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A total of 71 individual repeat elements representing 29 different families were upregulated in at least one heterochromatin mutant.
source: A total of 71 individual repeat elements representing 29 different families were upregulated in at least one mutant (Figure 3—source data 2; upregulation of 61/71 individual elements was confirmed based on uniquely mapping reads, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Calculated from RNA-seq differential expression analysis, data provided in Figure 3—source data 2.

claim: 41% of repetitive elements upregulated in heterochromatin mutants are upregulated in more than one mutant.
source: We observed a striking overlap in the sets of repetitive elements regulated by the heterochromatin factors: 41% of elements are upregulated in more than one mutant (Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Calculated from Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Seven repeat elements are upregulated in all five heterochromatin mutant strains, all of which are MIRAGE1 DNA transposable elements.
source: Furthermore, seven repeat elements are upregulated in all five strains, all of which are MIRAGE1 DNA transposable elements (Figure 3A,C,D, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by Venn diagram in Figure 3A and RNA-seq tracks in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority of repetitive elements upregulated in each heterochromatin mutant strain are DNA transposons, but retrotransposons are enriched for being upregulated.
source: The majority of repetitive elements upregulated in each heterochromatin mutant strain are DNA transposons, but retrotransposons are enriched for being upregulated (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by repeat class distribution analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MIRAGE1 RNA is abundant in the germ line of hpl-2, let-418, and lin-13 mutants but not in wild-type.
source: As expected from the RNA-seq results, wild-type adults had very low levels of MIRAGE1 RNA-FISH signal in germ line and soma (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3). In three tested heterochromatin mutants (hpl-2, let-418, and lin-13), we observed abundant germ line localized MIRAGE1 RNA whereas somatic expression remained low (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: RNAi knockdown of MIRAGE1 led to a small but significant increase in fertility of hpl-2, let-418, and lin-13 mutants.
source: Remarkably, RNAi of MIRAGE1 using mirage-A or mirage-B sets of RNAi clones led to a small but significant increase in fertility of all three mutants, showing that inappropriate MIRAGE1 expression contributes to their sterility (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Elements upregulated in any heterochromatin factor mutant are 83-fold enriched for containing a transposase.
source: We found that elements upregulated in any heterochromatin factor mutant are 83-fold enriched for containing a transposase (21 of 71) and 10-fold enriched for LTR retrotransposons (13 of 71), together accounting for nearly half of upregulated repeats.
evidence: Calculated from overlap analysis of upregulated repeats with transposase ORFs and LTR annotations.

claim: Elements upregulated in any heterochromatin factor mutant are 10-fold enriched for LTR retrotransposons.
source: We found that elements upregulated in any heterochromatin factor mutant are 83-fold enriched for containing a transposase (21 of 71) and 10-fold enriched for LTR retrotransposons (13 of 71), together accounting for nearly half of upregulated repeats.
evidence: Calculated from overlap analysis of upregulated repeats with LTR annotations.

claim: 267–513 genes are upregulated per heterochromatin mutant strain.
source: Consistent with roles in repression, we identified three to five times more genes with upregulated expression in each mutant strain compared to those with reduced expression (267–513 upregulated genes per mutant; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: Calculated from RNA-seq differential expression analysis, data provided in Figure 3—source data 3.

claim: Of the total set of 1155 genes upregulated in any of the five mutant strains, 404 are upregulated in more than one.
source: Additionally, there is a high degree of overlap among the upregulated genes; of the total set of 1155 genes upregulated in any of the five mutant strains, 404 are upregulated in more than one (Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: Calculated from overlap analysis of upregulated genes, data provided in Figure 3—source data 3.

claim: Heterochromatin factors are enriched at upregulated genes, but not downregulated genes (except for genes misregulated in let-418 mutants).
source: Heterochromatin factors are enriched at upregulated genes, but not downregulated genes (except for genes misregulated in let-418 mutants); additionally, both H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 are enriched at upregulated genes in all mutant strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: hpl-2 mutant germ lines show higher levels of oocyte fragmentation compared to wild type following ionizing radiation.
source: Following IR, we observed that hpl-2 mutants show higher levels of oocyte fragmentation compared to wild type, suggesting that they are defective in DNA repair (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by oocyte fragmentation assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: hpl-2 mutant germ lines are hypersensitive to induction of phosphorylation of the DNA damage checkpoint kinase CHK-1.
source: Additionally, hpl-2 mutant germ lines are hypersensitive to induction of phosphorylation of the DNA damage checkpoint kinase CHK-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by phospho-CHK-1 staining experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: hpl-2, lin-13, lin-61, and set-25 met-2 mutants all displayed increased germ line apoptosis.
source: We observed that hpl-2, lin-13, lin-61, and set-25 met-2 mutants all displayed increased germ line apoptosis (Figure 5; let-418 was not assayed because the apoptosis reporter used is genetically linked).
evidence: Demonstrated by CED-1::GFP apoptosis reporter experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RNAi of cep-1/p53 increased the brood sizes of hpl-2, lin-13, and let-418 mutants grown at 25°C.
source: Following RNAi of cep-1/p53, we found that the brood sizes of hpl-2, lin-13, and let-418 mutants grown at 25°C were modestly increased (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutation of cep-1 increased the fertility of lin-13, let-418 and hpl-2 mutants.
source: Similar to the RNAi results, we observed that mutation of cep-1 increased the fertility of lin-13, let-418 and hpl-2 mutants (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by double mutant brood size experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of cep-1 partially rescued the slow growth phenotype of hpl-2, let-418, and lin-13 mutants.
source: We also observed that cep-1 loss partially rescued the slow growth phenotype of the mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by developmental stage assessment shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Inhibiting meiotic double strand breaks by RNAi of spo-11 increased the brood size of hpl-2, lin-13, and let-418 mutants.
source: Similar to inhibition of damage induced cell death or MIRAGE1 expression, we found that inhibiting meiotic double strand breaks by RNAi of spo-11 increased the brood size of hpl-2, lin-13, and let-418 mutants (Figure 4A)
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 18 repetitive elements are upregulated in prg-1 mutants, 14 of which are also upregulated in at least one of the heterochromatin mutants, including MIRAGE1 elements.
source: We detected upregulation of 18 repetitive elements in prg-1 mutants, 14 of which are also upregulated in at least one of the heterochromatin mutants, including MIRAGE1 elements (Figure 6A, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq differential expression analysis and Venn diagram shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MIRAGE1 RNA is increased in prg-1 mutant germ lines.
source: RNA FISH experiments showed that MIRAGE1 RNA is increased in prg-1 mutant germ lines, similar to observations in heterochromatin mutants described above (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: prg-1 mutants show significantly increased germ cell death.
source: Indeed, we observed significantly increased germ cell death in prg-1 mutant adults (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by CED-1::GFP apoptosis reporter experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: lin-61 and let-418 mutants derepress the piRNA sensor reporter.
source: Similar to hpl-2 and set-25, we found that lin-61 and let-418 mutants derepress the piRNA sensor reporter (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by piRNA sensor expression assay shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: met-2 mutants show weak desilencing of the piRNA sensor in a fraction of adults.
source: We also observed weak desilencing in a fraction of met-2 mutants (Figure 6D), which was not observed in a previous assay (Ashe et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by piRNA sensor expression assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The piRNA sensor was not desilenced in lin-13 mutants.
source: However, the piRNA sensor was not desilenced in lin-13 mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by piRNA sensor expression assay shown in Figure 6D where lin-13 shows no significant difference from wild-type.

claim: hpl-2 mutants make normal levels of piRNAs.
source: Similar to the above results, we found that hpl-2 mutants make normal levels of piRNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by small RNA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Levels of 22G RNAs mapping near predicted piRNA target sites were normal in hpl-2 mutants.
source: We detected a decrease in 22G RNAs mapping near predicted piRNA target sites in prg-1 mutants as previously observed (Lee et al., 2012), but levels were normal in hpl-2 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by small RNA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: nrde-2 mutants showed a larger and different spectrum of repetitive element desilencing compared to prg-1 or any of the heterochromatin mutants.
source: We observed that nrde-2 mutants showed a larger and different spectrum of repetitive element desilencing compared to prg-1 or any of the heterochromatin mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Of 71 elements desilenced in nrde-2 mutants, only seven overlap a repeat desilenced in one of the heterochromatin mutant strains.
source: Of 71 elements desilenced in nrde-2 mutants, only seven overlap a repeat desilenced in one of the heterochromatin mutant strains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Calculated from Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MIRAGE1 elements are not desilenced in nrde-2 mutants.
source: Notably MIRAGE1 elements, prominently upregulated in heterochromatin and prg-1 mutants, are not desilenced in nrde-2 mutants (Figure 3—source data 1 and 2; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq tracks shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and data in Figure 3—source data 1 and 2.

claim: Retrotransposons are highly enriched among nrde-2 targets (45/71).
source: Retrotransposons are highly enriched among nrde-2 targets (45/71) whereas heterochromatin factors and prg-1 are more associated with DNA transposon misregulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Calculated from repeat class distribution analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 7C.

claim: nrde-2; let-418 double mutants showed a significantly smaller brood size than expected compared to the single mutants.
source: However, nrde-2; let-418, double mutants showed a significantly smaller brood size than expected compared to the single mutants, indicating partial functional redundancy between let-418 and the nrde pathway (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by double mutant brood size experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All three double mutants (nrde-2; hpl-2, nrde-2; lin-61, nrde-2; let-418) showed significantly increased embryo lethality compared to the single mutants.
source: We also observed that all three double mutants showed significantly increased embryo lethality compared to the single mutants (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by embryo lethality analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: More repeats are upregulated in nrde-2; let-418 double mutants compared to nrde-2 or let-418 single mutants.
source: We found that more repeats are upregulated in nrde-2; let-418 double mutants compared to nrde-2 or let-418 single mutants (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 7C (should be 7C, not 7B as stated in text).

claim: Most of the repeat elements upregulated only in the nrde-2; let-418 double mutant are retrotransposons (27/46).
source: Most of the repeat elements upregulated only in the nrde-2; let-418 double mutant are retrotransposons (27/46; Figure 7B and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Calculated from repeat class analysis of elements upregulated in nrde-2; let-418, data in Figure 3—source data 2.

claim: Repeat elements and genes upregulated in nrde-2 mutants have reduced H3K9me3 levels.
source: We observed that repeat elements and genes upregulated in nrde-2 mutants also have reduced H3K9me3 levels, supporting the link between H3K9me3 methylation and repression of endogenous targets (Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by H3K9me3 ChIP-seq analysis in nrde mutants shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: H3K9me3 was reduced on nrde-2 upregulated elements in mutants of other nrde genes that act in the germ line (hrde-1 and nrde-4), but not in the soma specific argonaute mutant nrde-3.
source: H3K9me3 was also reduced on nrde-2 upregulated elements in mutants of other nrde genes that act in the germ line (hrde-1 and nrde-4), but not in the soma specific argonaute mutant nrde-3 (Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by H3K9me3 ChIP-seq analysis in different nrde mutants shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Genes upregulated in any of the five heterochromatin factor mutant strains but not in nrde-2 mutants showed reduced H3K9me3 in germ line nrde mutants.
source: Indeed, genes upregulated in any of the five heterochromatin factor mutant strains (hpl-2, lin-13, let-418, lin-61, met-2 set-25) but not in nrde-2 mutants also showed reduced H3K9me3 in germ line nrde mutants, though the reduction was weaker than for nrde-2 regulated genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by H3K9me3 ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Repeats upregulated only in heterochromatin factor mutants showed a trend of reduced H3K9me3.
source: Repeats upregulated only in heterochromatin factor mutants showed a trend of reduced H3K9me3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by H3K9me3 ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The five heterochromatin factors each have unique and partially redundant germ line roles.
source: The fertility defects of single mutants and the enhancement in double loss of function combinations indicate that the five heterochromatin factors each have unique and partially redundant germ line roles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The genetic interactions among heterochromatin factors suggest that they may cooperate in a germ line process required for fertility.
source: The genetic interactions suggest that the five factors may cooperate in a germ line process required for fertility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A key role of heterochromatin factors is to suppress expression of repetitive element transposases.
source: Therefore, a key role of heterochromatin factors is to suppress expression of repetitive element transposases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of transposase-containing elements among upregulated repeats.

claim: One mechanism by which heterochromatin proteins promote normal germ line function is via the repression of repetitive elements, in particular those encoding transposases.
source: These results indicate that one mechanism by which heterochromatin proteins promote normal germ line function is via the repression of repetitive elements, in particular those encoding transposases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MIRAGE1 RNAi rescue experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Genotoxic stress and DNA damage signalling in heterochromatin mutants activates p53, which contributes to sterility and slow growth.
source: These results suggest that genotoxic stress and DNA damage signalling in heterochromatin mutants activates p53, which contributes to sterility and slow growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cep-1 suppression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Defects in repair of meiotic double strand breaks contributes to sterility of heterochromatin mutants.
source: Similar to inhibition of damage induced cell death or MIRAGE1 expression, we found that inhibiting meiotic double strand breaks by RNAi of spo-11 increased the brood size of hpl-2, lin-13, and let-418 mutants (Figure 4A), suggesting that defects in repair of meiotic double strand breaks contributes to sterility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spo-11 RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The piRNA pathway and heterochromatin factors have shared targets and phenotypes, and likely collaborate in maintaining genomic integrity of the developing germline.
source: Therefore, the piRNA pathway and heterochromatin factors have shared targets and phenotypes, and likely collaborate in maintaining genomic integrity of the developing germline.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap in upregulated repeats and increased apoptosis phenotypes.

claim: For hpl-2, the role in the piRNA pathway appears to be downstream of piRNA and subsequent 22G RNA synthesis.
source: Therefore, at least for hpl-2, the role in the piRNA pathway appears to be downstream of piRNA and subsequent 22G RNA synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small RNA analysis showing normal piRNA and 22G RNA levels in hpl-2 mutants.

claim: hpl-2, lin-61, let-418, set-25, and met-2 are important for piRNA pathway function.
source: To summarize, hpl-2, lin-61, let-418, set-25, and met-2 are important for piRNA pathway function.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the piRNA sensor desilencing experiments shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: The widespread binding sites and desilencing of additional targets relative to prg-1 indicate that heterochromatin proteins also mediate repression that is not piRNA-induced.
source: Nevertheless, the widespread binding sites and desilencing of additional targets relative to prg-1 indicate that heterochromatin proteins also mediate repression that is not piRNA-induced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of upregulated repeats in heterochromatin mutants versus prg-1 mutants.

claim: NRDE-2 and LET-418 have unique and redundant roles in the repression of repetitive DNA elements.
source: We conclude that NRDE-2 and LET-418 have unique and redundant roles in the repression of repetitive DNA elements.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction and RNA-seq data for nrde-2; let-418 double mutants shown in Figure 7.

claim: The germ line nuclear RNAi pathway partially controls H3K9me3 levels at loci regulated by heterochromatin factors.
source: Therefore, the germ line nuclear RNAi pathway partially controls H3K9me3 levels at loci regulated by heterochromatin factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the H3K9me3 ChIP-seq analysis in nrde mutants shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The observed reduction of H3K9me3 at heterochromatin-regulated loci in nrde mutants is not sufficient for derepression.
source: Because these elements are not upregulated in nrde-2 mutants, this indicates that the observed reduction of H3K9me3 is not sufficient for derepression and supports partial redundancy between the nrde pathway and heterochromatin factors in repeat silencing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that H3K9me3 is reduced but elements are not upregulated in nrde-2 mutants.

claim: Functional redundancy among factors and pathways underlies the importance of safeguarding the genome through multiple means.
source: Functional redundancy among factors and pathways underlies the importance of safeguarding the genome through multiple means.
evidence: This is a general conclusion stated in the abstract based on all the genetic interaction data.

claim: Heterochromatin factors may act locally within euchromatic domains rather than forming large heterochromatin domains.
source: We speculate that in many cases, repetitive element regulation involves a local mechanism rather than the spreading of large heterochromatin domains.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations that factor binding is closely associated with repeats and that genes containing bound repeats are often expressed.

claim: One fourth of genes contain a repetitive element bound by a heterochromatin factor.
source: Indeed, one fourth of genes contain a repetitive element bound by a heterochromatin factor, and of those, 59% (3287/5568) are expressed in the germ line.
evidence: This is calculated from the ChIP-seq and gene expression data.

claim: 59% of genes containing a repetitive element bound by a heterochromatin factor are expressed in the germ line.
source: Indeed, one fourth of genes contain a repetitive element bound by a heterochromatin factor, and of those, 59% (3287/5568) are expressed in the germ line.
evidence: This is calculated from the ChIP-seq and gene expression data.

claim: Defects in repair of DNA lesions are likely to cause germ line stress and to contribute to the germ line instability, germ line development defects, and increased germ line apoptosis seen in heterochromatin factor mutants.
source: Defects in repair of DNA lesions are likely to cause germ line stress and to contribute to the germ line instability, germ line development defects, and increased germ line apoptosis seen in heterochromatin factor mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DNA repair defects observed in heterochromatin mutants.

claim: Heterochromatin factors act to combat different types of genotoxic insults, both through silencing repetitive elements and facilitating repair.
source: These results suggest that heterochromatin factors act to combat different types of genotoxic insults, both through silencing repetitive elements and facilitating repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MIRAGE1 RNAi, spo-11 RNAi, and DNA repair defect data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Quality control mechanisms in the germ lines of heterochromatin factor mutants largely prevent improperly repaired meiotic germ cells from becoming mature gametes.
source: We propose that quality control mechanisms in the germ lines of heterochromatin factor mutants largely prevent improperly repaired meiotic germ cells from becoming mature gametes, either through apoptosis or the arrest of gametogenesis, to ensure that mutation rates are low.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that heterochromatin mutants do not show high embryo lethality or visible mutant phenotypes despite DNA damage.
